title: The deathbed test
hook: Ignatius suggests weighing your choice from your deathbed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rules for discernment: consolation, desolation, and making no change in the dark. Your line was read the heart. Which way did a strong mood try to pull you? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

There's a decision on the table. A job, a move, a yes or a no to someone. The list of pros and cons has been written twice, and it comes out even. Nothing inside is pulling hard either way. Ignatius has a tool for exactly this moment. Stop looking at the choice from where you're standing now, he says. Look at it from the very end of your life, from the bed you'll die in. It sounds grim. Some people find it oddly calming. Today: the deathbed test.
screen: `THE LIST COMES OUT EVEN.` → `NOTHING IS PULLING.` → `LOOK FROM THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: The deathbed test sits in the part of the Exercises about making a choice, which Ignatius calls an election. He describes three times when a person might choose. Sometimes God moves the will so clearly there's no doubting it. Sometimes the choice becomes clear through yesterday's movements, consolation and desolation. And sometimes it's a calm time, nothing stirring, and a person has to use their reason. For that calm time he offers a few tests. First, think of someone you've never met, whom you wish every good, and ask what you'd advise them to choose. Then follow your own advice. Second, today's test: consider, as if at the point of death, what you would then wish you had decided, and decide that way now. Third, picture yourself before God at the judgment and ask the same question. Notice what the deathbed does. It strips out the noise. The hope is that much of what pulls at a decision, what people will think, what's comfortable this year, goes quiet at the end, and what's left is simple. Did I love? Did I serve? Was I honest? An old line from the book of Ecclesiasticus, in the Douay-Rheims, puts it plainly: "In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin." This isn't meant to be morbid. Ignatius sets it right next to the stranger test, which is gentle and practical. Both do the same work: they lift you out of the middle of the moment and give you somewhere steadier to stand. It can work on small choices too. Whether to send the sharp email. Whether to call your mother back tonight.
screen: `AN ELECTION IS A CHOICE.` · `A CALM TIME NEEDS REASON.` · `ADVISE A STRANGER, THEN LISTEN.` · `WHAT WOULD I WISH, AT THE END?` · then, large: `REMEMBER THY LAST END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: test one decision. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one choice in front of you, big or small. Let the two options sit side by side. Now let time run forward, gently, to the end of a long life. You're old, and the room is quiet. Look back at this choice from there. Which way do you wish you had gone? Don't argue with the answer. Just notice it. Then come back to today, to the chair you're sitting in. If you pray, you can ask God for the courage to choose from there. The bell holds the time.
The deathbed test. Weighing a choice from the end of life, and deciding now the way you would wish you had then. Today's word.
Your line: from the end. Today, before one small decision, a reply, a purchase, a word to someone you love, look at it from the end, just for a breath. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: In Ignatian retreats and in spiritual direction, people facing a major decision in a calm time are invited to use Ignatius's tests, including advising a stranger and considering the choice as if at the point of death.

original.note: Spanish: election, a choice. Ignatius's word for a decision made before God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy thought experiment.
what it means: a way to make a calm decision, by asking what you'd wish you had chosen at the end.
what a scholar hears: it is one of the tests Ignatius gives for the third, calm time of election, alongside the stranger test and the judgment test.

sources.quoted: In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin.

sources.ref: Spiritual Exercises, three times for making an election (no. 175–177) and the second way of the third time (no. 184–187)

notes: Ecclesiasticus 7:40 is the Douay-Rheims (Vulgate) numbering; modern Bibles number it Sirach 7:36. Confirm the Douay-Rheims wording.
Paraphrases of the three times of election (nos. 175–177) and the rules of the second way (nos. 185–187: the stranger, the point of death, the day of judgment); confirm.
The index hook says 'imagines your choice from your deathbed'; the hook field is rephrased to avoid an 'Imagine' opening. Word and carry kept exactly.

Editor: 'strange' dropped (day 1250 and 1252 openers); 'it turns out to be oddly calming' no longer tells the listener what they will feel; the deathbed's effect hedged as Ignatius's hope rather than fact; 'On an ordinary Tuesday' replaced.
